title: LibreOffice says 'no AI' is now a software feature
content:
If you’re looking for a document editor that doesn’t use artificial intelligence, LibreOffice may be just the software for you.
The Document Foundation, the nonprofit software maker behind the open source document editor LibreOffice, said in a blog post this week that while it does not reject AI out of hand, it “will not add” AI to its software for the foreseeable future.
The blog post comes weeks after the release of the latest version of LibreOffice in late August, in which the nonprofit reiterated that the software “contains no generative AI features.”
LibreOffice said at the time that this was a “deliberate design position” to ensure that users’ documents are not uploaded to a server for processing and that no part of the software requires a network connection to function. The nonprofit added that its software is used by tens of millions of people and organizations, and that users should retain control over their data.
“Any organisation handling confidential, legally privileged or personal data needs to know where that data goes, and the only assurance that survives an audit is that it does not leave the machine,” the organization said.
LibreOffice says users can still choose to use AI tools by installing software extensions that connect the document editor to local AI models.
The decision to eschew including AI features bucks the trend of many software makers today that try to pack in as much AI as possible, even to the detriment of the user experience. The so-called “enshittification” of modern software by packing in unnecessary and bloated features, like chatbots and AI assistants, prompted some developers to create or include features that block or remove AI features altogether.
AI tools often require the users’ data to be uploaded and processed on a remote server, which the user has no control over how the data is stored or for how long.
LibreOffice said that there is currently “no integration” that meets all of its requirements, such as ensuring that the users’ data stays on their device and that there is no reliance on a single AI provider, among other considerations. The organization’s criteria for including AI into its software is not a “definitive rejection,” but the decision was an assessment of the technology today, rather than a “judgement on the value of the sector.”
“Until then, there will be no AI of any kind in the default installation; extensions will be available for those who wish to integrate AI features, and we will closely monitor where the technology is actually heading,” said LibreOffice’s blog post.
LibreOffice is one of the many kinds of open source and alternative software used to escape the clutches of Silicon Valley tech giants.

report.summary: LibreOffice will keep AI out of its default open-source office suite, offering extensions instead, to protect user data and control.
report.background: Productivity software has rushed to embed generative AI, from Microsoft 365 Copilot to Google Workspace Gemini, often processing documents in remote clouds. That shift has raised concerns about privacy, vendor lock-in, and 'enshittification'—bloated features users did not request. LibreOffice, maintained by the nonprofit Document Foundation, serves tens of millions of users and organizations, including those handling confidential, legally privileged, or personal data. In late August it reiterated that its latest release contains no generative AI and requires no network connection. Days later, it said it would not add AI for the foreseeable future, not as a rejection of AI's value but as a current assessment of integrations that fail its data-control and provider-independence tests.
key_points: LibreOffice's default installation will contain no AI of any kind for the foreseeable future. The Document Foundation calls this a deliberate design position: documents stay on the user's device, no network connection is required, and no generative AI features are included.

The nonprofit's main concern is data sovereignty. It argues that organizations handling confidential, legally privileged, or personal data need to know where data goes, and the only audit-proof assurance is that it never leaves the machine. This matters for legal, healthcare, government, and enterprise users.

Users who want AI can still opt in through extensions that connect LibreOffice to local AI models. This keeps the core software neutral while allowing experimentation, provided users accept responsibility for the extension's data handling and model choice.

The decision is not a permanent rejection. LibreOffice says no current integration meets all its criteria, including keeping data local and avoiding reliance on a single AI provider. It will monitor the technology and revisit if suitable options emerge.

LibreOffice is bucking an industry trend of adding chatbots and AI assistants to every app, sometimes harming usability. Its stance aligns with a broader privacy-first and anti-bloat movement, giving users a rare mainstream-like alternative with AI off by default.
report.impact: For the AI industry, LibreOffice's stance is a signal that not every software category will accept cloud AI by default. It could strengthen demand for on-device and private AI, pressuring vendors to offer offline, opt-in, and auditable features. For developers, it highlights architectural trade-offs: local models, extensions, and no single-provider lock-in become selling points rather than afterthoughts. For regular users, the benefit is choice and safer defaults, especially for sensitive documents; the cost is fewer native AI conveniences and more setup if they want assistance. Enterprises and public-sector buyers may see LibreOffice as easier to approve under strict data-governance rules.
report.tools: To follow up, watch LibreOffice's extension ecosystem for local AI connectors. Relevant open-source tools include Ollama, llama.cpp, LocalAI, GPT4All, and Jan for running models locally; Nextcloud Assistant and Open WebUI for private chat workflows. Also monitor the Document Foundation's blog for its evolving AI criteria and any future compliant integrations.
